youtube.baslik: Case: Asymmetric SNHL with Poor Word Recognition | Lesson 274 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
We assess a fictional adult case of asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss step by step: applying asymmetry criteria, a disproportionately poor word score and the rollover index, the reflex pattern and reflex decay, a sample ABR finding, ENT referral and report wording.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Hall, New Handbook of Auditory Evoked Responses; Jerger and Jerger, Diagnostic significance of PB word functions (1971); Dubno et al., Confidence limits for maximum word-recognition scores (1995).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Poor speech score and retrocochlear suspicion
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we work through an adult case with asymmetric sensorineural loss and a lower than expected word recognition score.
We will apply asymmetry criteria, read the rollover and reflex findings, and see the audiologist's role in referral for further testing.

maddeler.metin: Reduced hearing on the _left_ for a year
Now holds the phone to the right

cumleler: Our case is a fictional example: a fifty-two-year-old man comes in with reduced hearing in his left ear.
The complaint has been present for about a year and has grown slowly; he describes no sudden onset.
He noticed the loss when he could not understand speech after holding the phone to his left ear out of habit.
There is constant, high-pitched tinnitus in the left ear; there is no tinnitus in the right ear.
He describes an occasional mild feeling of unsteadiness, but no spinning attacks of vertigo.
There is no history of noise exposure, firearm use, ear surgery or head trauma.

sahneler.baslik: A *sensorineural* loss in the left ear
cumleler: Otoscopy is normal in both ears; right thresholds slope slightly toward the high frequencies and can be considered age-related.
In the left ear there is a loss that grows clearly above 1000 hertz; thresholds are 50 dB HL at 2000 hertz and 65 dB HL at 8000 hertz.
Left bone conduction, measured with the right ear masked, overlaps air conduction, so the loss is sensorineural.
Had it been measured unmasked, left bone conduction might have come from the right cochlea, showing a false air-bone gap.
Testing used insert earphones; left air minus right bone conduction stayed below interaural attenuation, so no masking was needed.
The picture is consistent with an asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear.
Now let us test whether this asymmetry is significant with the criteria we saw in an earlier lesson.
A commonly used criterion counts a difference of 15 dB or more at two adjacent frequencies as significant.
In our case the difference is 30 dB at 2000 hertz and again 30 dB at 3000 hertz; the criterion is met.
The 3000 rule, which looks only at 3000 hertz, also has its 15 dB limit clearly exceeded.
In protocols looking for 20 dB at a single frequency, the 35 dB difference at 4000 hertz is also enough.
So whichever criterion we use, this asymmetry is significant; the report names the criterion used.
The history has no noise, trauma or ear disease to explain the asymmetry, and one-sided tinnitus and unsteadiness come with it.
When an asymmetry is found, the first question is whether a known cause can explain it; for example, one-sided noise exposure.
Past chronic ear disease or ear surgery can also cause more loss in one ear.
Meniere's disease or an earlier sudden hearing loss can also leave a one-sided sensorineural loss.
Our case has none of these causes, which makes the asymmetry an unexplained finding.
Even when a known cause is found, referral is still made if the explanation is not enough.
An unexplained asymmetry may call for imaging of the internal auditory canal or the cerebellopontine angle.
In this region the cochlear nerve, the vestibular nerves and the facial nerve run side by side.
The most common tumor here is the vestibular schwannoma, which arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve.
The tumor is benign and usually grows slowly; as it grows it can press on the cochlear nerve and the cochlea's blood supply.
One-sided loss, one-sided tinnitus and mild unsteadiness are among the most common signs of this tumor.
But most of these signs also have other causes; the audiologist notes the possibility, while the physician and imaging make the diagnosis.
The right word recognition score is 96 percent, consistent with the degree of loss.
In the left ear, with the right ear masked, scores were measured at several levels; this curve is a performance-intensity function.
The highest left score is 60 percent, at 75 dB HL.
For an ear with a pure-tone average of about 37 dB, this score is clearly lower than expected.
When the level rises to 90 dB HL the score drops to 28 percent; a falling score at high levels is called rollover.
The rollover index is the difference between the highest and lowest scores divided by the highest: sixty minus twenty eight, over sixty.
The result is about zero point five three, above the zero point four five criterion proposed for the Jerger and Jerger lists.

sahneler.baslik: What does a low score *tell us?*
cumleler: A word score that is disproportionately low for the degree of loss is a retrocochlear warning sign.
Marked rollover at high levels points the same way; in cochlear losses the score is usually maintained at high levels.
The confidence limits published by Dubno and colleagues show the lowest expected score for a given pure-tone average.
For this comparison to be valid, recorded material must be used and the opposite ear must be masked at a suitable level.
Still, scores can fluctuate on short lists, and rollover is not seen in every retrocochlear problem; the finding is part of the battery.
Tympanograms are type A in both ears; the middle ear systems are normal.
With the stimulus in the right ear, reflexes are at expected levels in both ipsilateral and contralateral measures.
With the stimulus in the left ear, there is no reflex at 1000 and 2000 hertz; at 500 hertz it appears only at 90 dB HL.
The left threshold at 1000 hertz is 35 dB HL; a cochlear loss of this degree does not usually abolish the reflex.
An absent or elevated reflex when the affected ear receives the stimulus suggests a problem in the sensory limb of the reflex arc.
This pattern is consistent with the retrocochlear pattern we saw in the lesson on reflex patterns.
At 500 hertz, where a left reflex was present, a decay test was done: a ten-second tone 10 dB above the reflex threshold.
The dashed gray line shows amplitude maintained for ten seconds in a normal ear.
In the left ear, amplitude falls quickly within a few seconds and drops below half at about four seconds.
Amplitude falling below half within ten seconds is positive reflex decay and suggests retrocochlear pathology.
A negative result would not rule out a retrocochlear problem; the finding is always interpreted as part of the battery.
Let us bring the findings together: an unexplained sensorineural asymmetry, confirmed with masking and significant on every criterion.
A word score disproportionately low for the degree of loss, with marked rollover.
Absent or elevated reflexes when the left ear is stimulated, and positive reflex decay.
These come with one-sided tinnitus and mild unsteadiness in the same ear.
None of these findings is conclusive alone, but together they strongly support looking for a retrocochlear cause.
The first step is to verify the asymmetry: is masking adequate, and are the thresholds the same on retest?
The report clearly includes the asymmetry criterion used, the speech and reflex findings and the accompanying symptoms.
The person is referred to an ENT physician with the findings; the referral note asks for assessment from a retrocochlear standpoint.

cumleler.yazi: The physician decides on imaging and method; the gold standard is magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, with contrast or special sequences.
cumleler.ses: The physician decides on imaging and method; the gold standard is magnetic resonance imaging, or M R I, with contrast or special sequences.

cumleler: In some centers, the auditory brainstem response, or ABR, is also added to the battery according to protocol.
The audiologist checks whether the person reached the physician and schedules a follow-up visit.

notlar.metin: A normal ABR does not replace MRI

cumleler: Let us look at a sample ABR recording made according to the center's protocol.

cumleler.yazi: In the right ear, waves I, III and V are at expected latencies; the I-V interval is about four milliseconds.
cumleler.ses: In the right ear, waves one, three and five are at expected latencies; the one to five interval is about four milliseconds.

cumleler.yazi: In the left ear, wave I is visible but wave V is delayed; the I-V interval is about 4.8 milliseconds.
cumleler.ses: In the left ear, wave one is visible but wave five is delayed; the one to five interval is about 4.8 milliseconds.

cumleler.yazi: If the I-V interval exceeds about 4.4 to 4.5 milliseconds, a retrocochlear delay is suggested.
cumleler.ses: If the one to five interval exceeds about 4.4 to 4.5 milliseconds, a retrocochlear delay is suggested.

cumleler: Remember: with small tumors the ABR can be normal; a normal ABR does not replace imaging.

cumleler.yazi: This result is not a diagnosis either; it is an additional finding that supports the physician's MRI decision.
cumleler.ses: This result is not a diagnosis either; it is an additional finding that supports the physician's M R I decision.

sahneler.metin: Do not play down the asymmetry, and do not alarm the person either; explain the finding clearly and always check that they saw the physician.
cumleler: A clinical tip: when making the referral, speak without alarming the person, but without playing down the finding.
For example, you can say: the difference between your ears is larger than expected; your physician's assessment matters to find out why.
Words like tumor or cancer, or percentages of likelihood, are not things for the audiologist to say.
Asking whether the person went to the appointment makes sure the referral reaches an outcome.

maddeler.metin: No reflex with left stimulus, decay

cumleler: Pure tones: left mild to moderate sensorineural hearing loss increasing toward high frequencies; right ear consistent with age.
Asymmetry: significant by our clinic protocol's criterion of 15 dB at two adjacent frequencies.
Speech: left word recognition score disproportionately low for the loss; rollover index zero point five three.
Immittance: type A tympanograms; reflexes absent or elevated with left stimulation, positive reflex decay at 500 hertz.
Recommendation: referral to an ENT physician for retrocochlear assessment, and a follow-up audiogram when the physician sees fit.

cumleler.yazi: If the MRI is normal, the person may still be followed audiologically at set intervals to see whether the loss progresses.
cumleler.ses: If the M R I is normal, the person may still be followed audiologically at set intervals to see whether the loss progresses.

cumleler: If a tumor is found, the medical team weighs options such as monitoring, surgery or radiotherapy.
Throughout this process, the audiologist documents the course of hearing with serial audiograms and speech scores.

cumleler.yazi: Depending on remaining hearing and the speech score, a hearing aid or a CROS system that routes sound to the other side can be discussed.
cumleler.ses: Depending on remaining hearing and the speech score, a hearing aid or a cross system that routes sound to the other side can be discussed.

cumleler: Since a low speech score can limit the expected benefit of a device, expectations are discussed realistically from the start.

maddeler.metin: Report asymmetry by the criterion's name

cumleler: Asymmetric sensorineural loss is confirmed with masking and reported with the name of the criterion used.
A word score disproportionately low for the loss, and rollover, are retrocochlear warning signs.
Absent reflexes when the affected ear is stimulated, and positive reflex decay, point the same way.
The physician decides on imaging; the audiologist's role is to verify the finding, report it and follow up on the referral.

sahneler.soru: The ABR is normal. What does it mean?
secenekler: It does not rule out a small tumor
sahneler.aciklama: With small tumors the ABR _can be normal_; the imaging decision is the physician's.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a person with asymmetric loss, the ABR is normal. What does this result mean?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: it does not rule out a small tumor.

cumleler.yazi: The ABR has low sensitivity for small tumors; the gold standard is MRI, and the physician decides on imaging.
cumleler.ses: The ABR has low sensitivity for small tumors; the gold standard is M R I, and the physician decides on imaging.
